senses: Resembling or characteristic of a dog.
Resembling a mongrel dog, notably in its worst qualities.
Stylish in a showy way.
ety: From Middle English doggische, doggissh; equivalent to dog + -ish.
examples: The show's high point is Jim Nutt's "Pug," an image of a woman whose slightly doggish face and coiled hair has all the concentrated perfection of a Northern Renaissance portrait.

senses: Characteristic of a traitor; disloyal.
ety: From Middle English trayterous, traytrous, (also Middle English traytours, treytours), from Anglo-Norman traiterous, traitourous and Old French traitros.

senses: A card, die, or domino with five spots or pips.
ety: From Middle English cynk, from Middle French cinq, from Latin cīnque, variant of quīnque. The archaic spelling cinq is taken from modern French cinq, whereas the standard spelling is perhaps influenced by Italian cinque or a misspelling of the French. The variant pronunciation /sæŋk/ is based on Modern French. Doublet of fin (“five currency units”), finnuf, five, pimp (“five”), ponzu, punch (“beverage”), and sengi (“currency”); related to Pompeii.

senses: An upward thrust.
a plate, made by electroplating a mold, such as used in letterpress printing
A Japanese rice bowl dish consisting of fish, meat, vegetables or other ingredients served together over rice.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 丼 (donburi, “a large helping of rice covered in meat, fish, and/or vegetables, all served in one big bowl”).

senses: An exegesis.
ety: Borrowed from Hebrew or Aramaic דְּרַשׁ.

senses: A still (non-carbonated), typically homemade or fresh-squeezed drink made of water, lemon juice, and sweetener.
Having or existing in a single shape or form.
To make or give the appearance of being glamorous.
To glorify; to romanticize.
examples: Some movies glamorize criminal activity by making criminals seem cool.

senses: A type of spiced shortcrust biscuit.
The Belgian version of this biscuit, as contrasted with a Dutch speculaas or German Spekulatius.
A type of spread made with the biscuit.
ety: From Dutch speculoos, Flemish form of speculaas.

senses: Any plant of the family Cyperaceae.
ety: From Middle English segge, from Old English seċġ, from Proto-West Germanic *sagi, from Proto-Germanic *sagjaz, from Proto-Indo-European *sak- (“marsh plant”). Cognate with Dutch zegge and German Segge, dialectal German Saher (“reeds”).

senses: An ancient Greek or Roman building used for performances of music and poetry.
A theatre or concert hall.
ety: From Ancient Greek ᾠδεῖον (ōideîon), from ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”) + -εῖον (-eîon, noun-forming suffix meaning “place or building associated with a specific purpose or person”).

senses: A leather strap or thong which is split into (typically three) tails, used for corporal punishment in schools, applied to the palm of the hands or buttocks.
ety: Apparently a plural form of taw, though attested earlier.

senses: The establishment or furnace that cremates bodies.
The extent to which something is granular.
Used as, or relating to, a motif.
examples: In fact, Tucker's use of parallel motion and open fourths as a central motivic element particularly reminded me of Stravinsky's sacred music, especially the quieter sections of Symphony of Psalms and the Mass.

senses: To waste, especially time.
Forming an adjunct.
Forming a noun adjunct.
Additional; neither basic nor primary.
Between sectors.
examples: The byproducts of our study are a strategy to improve the change and project management in intersectoral collaboration and a large repertoire of managerial working methods and instruments.

senses: A (Finnish) mark, the currency used in Finland before the introduction of the euro, consisting of 100 penni. Abbreviation FIM.
ety: Borrowed from Finnish markka, from a Germanic language, likely German Mark. Doublet of mark.

senses: A motorbike capable of levitation.
A person or thing that fetches something
ety: From Middle English fecchere, equivalent to fetch + -er.
examples: More and more people agreed to help with the mailings, the hand-distribution of flyers, and telephonings. Others agreed to be gofers and fetchers.

senses: American and Oxford British English standard spelling of sodomise.
examples: Antonio thus "actively" sodomized the presumably adolescent Lorenzo by fellating him

senses: A shape composed of three equilateral triangles arranged in such a manner that a fourth triangle of identical size, but pointing the opposite direction, could fit between them.
ety: From Japanese トライフォース (toraifōsu), from English tri- + force. First used in the Legend of Zelda video game franchise for a magical artefact in that fictional universe.

senses: Trusting; willing to trust.
ety: From Middle English trustful, trystefull, equivalent to trust + -ful.

senses: A French infantryman during the First World War
ety: Borrowed from French poilu (“brave”). Doublet of plew.

senses: The ability to be customized.
A highly contagious form of conjunctivitis.
Kagome Kagome, a Japanese children's game.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 籠目 (かごめ, kagome).

senses: A ritual, rooted in the Vedic religion, in which offerings of food etc. are burnt in order to bring good luck on a special occasion.

The main component of the rear suspension of most modern motorcycles and ATVs; holds the rear axle in place while swinging vertically to allow the suspension to absorb the shock from bumps in the road.
examples: At the rear, you'll find a single, centrally mounted shock, the now-familiar single-sided swingarm and BMW's Paralever shaft-drive system, which does away with most of a shafty's chassis-jacking bugaboos.
At the rear, stiffer springs, a new aluminum swingarm and a redesigned linkage for the suspension all benefit on-road behavior, though there is now an inch less ground clearance.

senses: Prickly; spiny.
A person or thing that descends.
The part of a letter or number that is drawn below the baseline (the bottom of most lowercase letters).
A letter that has such a portion, such as g, j, or in some fonts Q.
Synonym of floppy.
examples: They had flopsy hair, tucked their frayed tailored trousers into their boots, carried flasks in their moleskin blazers and never looked as if they were trying too hard.

senses: To spin around or about, so as to cover; spin all over.
ety: From be- + spin. Cognate with German bespinnen (“to spin over”).
examples: Here we still have much of the same authority of great texts bespun and sometimes swamped with glosses and notes, of lecturing that approximates dictation, and grammar which still remains, though dictionaries have come.

senses: The state of being neutral; neutrality.
A political policy of nonalignment in a situation of conflict.
A Sicilian dish of baked aubergines with capers, olives, pine nuts etc, normally served cold.
A music note typically equal to two longae (eight semibreves).
ety: From Latin maxima (“greatest”). Doublet of maxim.

senses: A plebeian, a member of the lower class of Roman citizens.
ety: From Latin plēbs (“the plebeian class”), probably via Middle French plebe (“plebeians, commoners, the rabble”) and possibly later understood as a clipping of plebeian. Cognate with Italian plebe, Spanish plebe, Portuguese plebe.
